A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FlexMerge work. Their main text, equations, algorithms, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable, and relocated or renumbered material can be reliably matched.

before.justification: V1 reports original vision, NLP and multimodal experiments, merging ablations, and merging/inference latency measurements.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds TSV-M evaluations, held-out-task results and an additional selection ablation.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the minimum-cosine greedy merging rule remain unchanged. V2 Appendix C.6 adds an inference extension for unseen tasks: predictions ensemble the eight in-domain branches, whereas the existing task-specific inference procedure follows one branch. The DSU description concerns implementation rather than a changed merging rule.

E1.justification: V2 Appendix C.6 adds held-out-task evaluation on Weather, PCAM, Flowers102, Landscapes, Beans and Food101 using models merged from eight other tasks. These datasets already participated in v1's 30-task benchmark, but their use as unseen tasks introduces a distinct generalization scenario. Existing vision, NLP and multimodal coverage is retained.

E2.justification: TSV-M is newly evaluated alongside the existing mergers on the eight- and 30-task vision benchmarks with both ViT models (v2 Figures 8–9). The new OOD comparison also evaluates individual source experts against FlexMerge. Both TA and TIES comparisons with Channel Merging existed in v1 and are retained after relocation.

E3.justification: V2 introduces the eight-source/six-held-out-task protocol with branch ensembling and adds a 30-task Consensus selection experiment. The TA comparison with Channel Merging changes from average normalized accuracy in v1 Figure 14 to raw average accuracy in v2 Figure 5. Existing training settings and the inference-batch experiment remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 substantially extends the analytical scope with held-out-task generalization tests and explicit comparisons of ranking stability across model sizes on vision, PEFT and FFT benchmarks. Figure 19 also adds cosine-versus-random selection for Consensus on 30 tasks. Conversely, v1's 5.05× clustering case study is removed; the 2.16× example and the relocated scaling analysis remain.

E5.justification: Table 3 retains the same ± timing summaries, and the existing shaded uncertainty displays remain. V2 introduces no stated changes to seed counts, repeated-run counts, uncertainty estimation or significance testing; the additional ablation follows the existing display practice.

E6.justification: V2 adds TSV-M curves, OOD results and ranking findings across sizes. For example, Tables 5–6 report ViT-B/32 OOD accuracy of 0.6410 at 1.5× versus 0.6366 for the best individual expert. Table 2 replaces FlexMerge timings of approximately 10/491 seconds for eight/30 tasks with 2.3/20 seconds, now explicitly labeled as covering all sizes. These are revised reported timings; the principal retained accuracy curves are unchanged.

T1.justification: The shared-architecture assumption, task-vector definitions, minimum-cosine similarity definition and reconstruction equations (1–6) are unchanged. Neither version adds formal guarantees or proofs relative to the other.

C1.justification: V1 centers its contributions on flexible model sizes and favorable accuracy-size trade-offs. V2 adds algorithm-ranking reversals as a second central finding in the abstract and introduction, explicitly arguing for developing and comparing merging algorithms beyond the single-model regime. This substantively broadens the paper's main scientific message.

C2.justification: V2 interprets ranking changes as motivation for algorithm development across sizes and the new held-out results as evidence that FlexMerge can improve OOD generalization. The architectural and theoretical limitations remain unchanged. V1's explanation linking TIES degradation to increasing sign conflicts, and its broader-impact discussion, are omitted.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents Disjoint Set Union bookkeeping in Section 3.2 and TSV-M's treatment of 2D parameters with singular vectors and 1D parameters with averaging in Appendix B.1. Table 2 clarifies that FlexMerge timings cover all sizes. V1's explicit statement that CLIP's text encoder remains fixed is dropped; hardware and the other existing training details are retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds Gargiulo et al.'s TSV-M work and Cormen et al.'s algorithms reference, while removing the original Hu et al. LoRA citation. The Channel Merging discussion emphasizes its inability to produce fractional sizes. Most prior-work coverage remains; consolidating appendix references and changing citation style are presentation changes.

P1.justification: The abstract and contribution list are substantially rewritten, and the experimental narrative is reorganized from six subsections into three. Vision and NLP results are consolidated, scaling analysis moves to the appendix, and ablations and efficiency are grouped together. Appendix references are integrated into the main bibliography, and the broader-impact section is removed.

P2.justification: V2 redraws Figure 1, replacing the hypothetical trade-off panel with measured algorithm comparisons, and rebuilds Figure 5 around the moved TA comparison and new ranking displays. It splits the appendix vision figure to accommodate TSV-M, adds OOD tables, removes the 5.05× cluster display and substantially reformats the algorithm and document layout. Figure 4's caption also corrects the PEFT interval to 1×–3× without changing its plotted results.

improvement.justification: V2 makes comparisons across model sizes clearer, extends evidence with TSV-M and held-out-task evaluations, documents an efficiency detail, and fixes Figure 4's misleading PEFT caption. These provide useful incremental gains over an already extensive empirical paper. The OOD comparison ensembles eight branches against individual experts, limiting attribution of its advantage specifically to merging, so the added evidence supports a limited overall improvement.
